strengths: Identifies a novel and important incompatibility between curriculum learning and LR decay that explains prior limited success—a genuine insight previously overlooked
Comprehensive experimental validation with systematic ablations on ending LR values clearly demonstrating the effect across multiple schedules and quality metrics
Practical and implementable solutions that integrate with existing data preprocessing pipelines without requiring additional scoring steps
Clear presentation with effective visualizations (especially Figures 1, 4) and intuitive signal/noise interpretation of the mechanism
Demonstrates larger improvements in practical mid-training setting (1.2-2% on core benchmarks), suggesting real-world applicability
Thorough ablations across datasets (DCLM, WebOrganizer, PreSelect), architectures, and model averaging strategies show robustness within tested scope
Provides actionable guidelines for practitioners regarding optimal LR schedules for curriculum-based training (~1×10⁻³ vs 1×10⁻⁵)
Formal theoretical analysis in Section 6 with bounds showing improvement from Θ(L²) to Õ(M^{-2/3}L²)
weaknesses: Limited experimental scale (1.5B parameters with 30B tokens) raises questions about generalization to modern large-scale settings (7B, 70B+ models)
Modest absolute improvements (1.64% average, 2% on core benchmarks) without statistical significance testing or confidence intervals reported
PreSelect ablation shows curriculum underperforming uniform ordering on validation loss, partially contradicting main claims and suggesting metric/dataset dependence
Theoretical model in Section 6 is highly simplified (2D quadratic loss, evenly-distributed data) with unclear connection to practical ~1-2% improvements in complex neural networks
Validation set uses DCLM-scored documents while curriculum sorts by DCLM scores—potential circularity that could bias results
Solutions are largely incremental: moderate LR decay is straightforward parameter tuning; model averaging is prior work (Izmailov et al., 2018; Tian et al., 2025)
Limited investigation of failure cases: folding strategy dismissal is somewhat superficial; PreSelect underperformance not deeply analyzed
No computational cost analysis: sorting overhead, checkpoint storage, and averaging time for production systems not quantified
Missing statistical rigor: single runs reported without error bars; ~1-2% improvements could be within noise without significance testing
Unclear how findings scale to multi-phase training beyond 2-phase setup, generation tasks, or different optimizer/architecture choices

strengths: Well-motivated identification of incompatibility between curriculum learning and LR decay schedules with clear empirical demonstration (Figure 1)
Comprehensive experimental validation at substantial scale (1.5B params, 30B tokens) with thorough ablations across multiple quality metrics and datasets
Practical solutions (moderate LR decay and model averaging) that are simple to implement and integrate into existing pipelines without additional overhead
Solid theoretical grounding with loss landscape intuition (Section 4), though limited in scope
Extensive reproducibility support with complete hyperparameters and detailed experimental methodology
Large-scale validation on continual pretraining (3.2B model, 150B+ tokens) demonstrating applicability to practical scenarios
Clear presentation of the core phenomenon with good visualizations of data quality vs LR schedule mismatch
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty—combines well-established components (moderate decay, model averaging, curriculum learning) without introducing fundamentally new methods
Oversimplified theoretical analysis using 2D quadratic loss that poorly captures LLM training dynamics; weak connection between asymptotic bounds and practical 30B token scale
Moderate and variable empirical improvements (1.64% average, ranging from -0.78% to +3.39% across benchmarks; failures on mathematical reasoning and coding tasks)
Incomplete mechanistic understanding: paper doesn't rigorously explain why LR decay specifically hurts curriculum learning or why weight averaging helps despite claiming these as main contributions
Quality metric dependency not adequately addressed—PreSelect experiments show worse validation loss than uniform ordering, contradicting main narrative; suggests fragility to metric choice
Significant hyperparameter sensitivity with optimal ending LR differing dramatically between curriculum (1×10⁻³) and uniform (1×10⁻⁵) training, requiring different tuning strategies
Insufficient ablation decomposing improvement sources between curriculum ordering and model averaging effects
Title's claim about 'wasting' data is overstated—method diminishes rather than wastes high-quality data
